learning_outcomes.text: Students can analyze energy technology issues holistically, systematically, and quantitatively under technical, economic, and climate aspects.
Quantify energy technology plants and systems with energy flow diagrams, describing all relevant energy flows mathematically and calculating energy yields.
Know and apply efficiencies and utilization rates for various energy conversion technologies to describe, analyze, and compare chained or coupled systems.

Understand the effective and loss mechanisms of energy conversion processes and thus evaluate and compare conversion concepts or energy generation plants based on metrics such as energy density, resource input/land requirement, and CO2 intensity, and estimate possible future potential.

Know the basics of heat, electrical energy, and chemical energy (gas) transport and transmission, estimate or calculate losses and other transport properties, and thus analyze and evaluate various energy distribution concepts.

Recognize the problem of electrical energy storage and its importance for grid stability, classify storage concepts based on fundamental storage characteristics, identify sensible application areas, and develop solution concepts.
Economically analyze energy technology plants and systems by applying financial mathematical methods and formulas, calculate profitability and costs, and justify investment decisions and pricing.

Recognize and qualitatively estimate and predict the influence of external events and energy policy decisions on energy prices through their learned understanding of market-based price formation mechanisms.

Roughly dimension energy technology plants and systematically evaluate techno-economic energy concepts in a professional environment, and as engineers, contribute to a factual and evidence-based discussion in the energy policy context.

syllabus_topics: Motivation: connection between energy and climate problem, societal importance of energy technology, climate neutrality
Connection between energy conversion and CO2 emissions, technology-specific emission factors
Fundamentals: balance equations, concept of exergy and anergy, heat transfer modes, energy technology and energy economics terms
Concept of energy flow diagrams: creation and application for generic balance-like description of energy conversion processes

Operating mechanisms, conversion efficiencies, operating characteristics and rough design/dimensioning of the most relevant CO2-minimal energy conversion technologies (according to IPCC AR5 life cycle emissions), e.g.:
Solar energy conversion (photovoltaic and solar thermal)
Line-bound energy transport of heat, electricity and gas: description of transport properties, components, rough quantification of transport losses
Storage problem with focus on electrical energy: power balance equation, storage options and storage properties, application areas
Economic evaluation of energy generation plants: investment cost accounting, levelized cost of electricity
Pricing and trading of energy: energy exchange, merit-order principle, price components for end consumers
Evaluation, discussion of current energy policy topics
assessment_rules: The assessment will be either a 90-minute written examination or a 20-minute oral examination. The specific examination format will be announced at the beginning of the course.
